one_liner: Compressed static DNA k-mer dictionary: ~5x smaller than Pufferfish, 1.6-2.4x faster streaming lookups, but slower random lookups.
what_it_does: SSHash stores a static set of DNA k-mers (k <= 31 by default, <= 63 with a compile flag) and answers Lookup (k-mer to a dense ID in [0,n), or -1), Access (ID to k-mer), membership, streaming lookups over FASTA/FASTQ reads, and de Bruijn graph neighbour queries; optional per-k-mer weights (abundances) are stored compressed. A k-mer and its reverse complement count as the same key, and each result reports which strand matched plus the containing string (unitig) ID and offset. Input is a spectrum-preserving string set (unitigs or eulertigs from BCALM2, GGCAT or Cuttlefish), not raw reads. You use it through the `sshash` CLI (build/query/bench/permute) or the C++ `sshash::dictionary` class from a CMake static-library target; the API is its own, not a map or MPHF interface.
how_it_is_fast: Sparse and skew hashing: consecutive k-mers of the input strings are grouped into super-k-mers by their minimizer, and a PTHash minimal perfect hash is built over the distinct minimizers only (about 6.5x fewer keys than k-mers at k=31, m=20 in the 2022 paper), so a lookup hashes the minimizer to a small bucket of offsets into the 2-bit-packed strings and verifies the k-mer against the text instead of storing k-mers. Singleton buckets resolve with one text comparison, buckets with fewer than 2^6 super-k-mers are scanned, and the rare heavy buckets go to a 'skew index' of per-size-class PTHash functions over the k-mers themselves, which caps string accesses. Streaming queries skip hashing while a read follows a stored string: after a hit the next query k-mer is compared with the next k-mer of the same unitig ('extension'), and v6 memoizes the last minimizer's bucket to shortcut negatives. Since v6 a forward minimizer scheme with a centre-closest tie-break puts a k-mer and its reverse complement in the same bucket, so every lookup is a single probe.
when_to_use: Static sets of 10^8 to 10^10 DNA k-mers (bacterial pangenomes, human, HPRC) built from unitigs/eulertigs, where you need k-mer-to-ID and ID-to-k-mer, e.g. as the k-mer index inside a read mapper (the repo carries merged PRs for submodule integration into COMBINE-lab's piscem).

Streaming membership over FASTQ reads, where consecutive k-mers overlap: v6 measures 76 ns/k-mer on Human k=31 (high-hit), against 266 ns for SBWT and 1,176 ns for FMSI on the same hardware in jermp/kmer_sets_benchmark.
Memory-constrained indexing: 7.4-10.6 bits/k-mer at k=31 and 3.8-7.6 at k=63 in the current benchmarks (2.75 GB for human k=31), with an --mmap option to query the index from disk.
Workloads that need Access (rank to k-mer) or navigational queries: Access takes 0.35 us/k-mer on Human k=31, against 10.81 us for SBWT and 18.62 us for FMSI.
Pipelines that rebuild often: human k=31 builds in 2:35 with 64 threads under a 16 GB RAM cap, using an external-memory builder with a RAM limit (-g) and a temp directory (-d).
when_not_to_use: Isolated random point lookups with RAM to spare: in the 2022 paper Pufferfish dense answered them faster (720/519 ns positive/negative vs 990/854 ns) while using about 5x the space (45.04 vs 9.39 bits/k-mer).
When the smallest index matters most: FMSI takes 3.2-4.4 bits/k-mer at k=31, against 7.4-10.6 for SSHash, though its lookups and streaming queries are more than 10x slower.
Dynamic sets: the index is immutable, so any insert or delete means a full rebuild.

Raw reads or sequences with duplicate or non-ACGT k-mers: the README requires deduplicated, N-free, one-sequence-per-line input, so you must run GGCAT/BCALM2 first. For membership-only use on inputs with duplicate k-mers (e.g. matchtigs), the author points to SSHash-Lite.
General keys or tiny sets: it is not a general hash map or MPHF (use PTHash directly for that), and the author says the smallest input worth indexing is a single bacterial genome (issue #33).

integration.dependencies: PTHash (git submodule, which brings bits, essentials, fastmod, xxHash and mm_file), zlib; CityHash vendored in external/
integration.min_toolchain: C++17, CMake 3.5+; CI builds with GCC 11-14 and Clang 16-18 on Ubuntu; k up to 63 needs __uint128_t (GCC/Clang)
integration.platforms: x86-64 (CMake always adds -mavx2 -mbmi2, so AVX2/BMI2 CPUs are required) and aarch64 (builds since the Sep 2025 fix for issue #77); tested on Linux with gcc and macOS with clang; Windows not documented
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Build is multi-threaded (-t) with a RAM cap. The dictionary's query methods are const; streaming_query keeps mutable per-stream state, so use one per thread. All published query benchmarks are single-threaded.

gotchas: The builder does not screen its input: build with the same k that produced the unitigs, and supply deduplicated, ACGT-only sequences with one per line. Use --check to verify the built index.

The default 2-bit nucleotide encoding is non-standard (A=00, C=01, T=10, G=11), so passing packed-integer k-mers from other tools needs -DSSHASH_USE_TRADITIONAL_NUCLEOTIDE_ENCODING=On. Max k (31 or 63) is also fixed at compile time.

Performance and size depend on the minimizer length m, which you must choose. The builder prints a warning only in --verbose mode when m < ceil(log4(N))+1, and the benchmarks tune m per dataset (19-21 for k=31, 23-31 for k=63).
The index format is versioned: v6.0.0 (Aug 2026) removed the canonical/regular modes, and loading an index with a different major version throws 'SSHash index needs rebuilding'.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Over RSHash, which claims 1.4x faster streaming on average, pick SSHash for maturity and features: Bioconda packaging, a Rust port, releases since 2022, navigational queries, compressed weights and k up to 63 (RSHash has 8 stars, and its README builds with g++-14 and seqan3). Over BLight, pick SSHash when space and query speed matter: in the 2022 paper it used 9.39 vs 20.17 bits/k-mer and was faster on both streaming and random lookups, though BLight's build peaked at less RAM (7.5 vs 17.3 GB).
verified_claims_summary: In the 2022 Bioinformatics paper (gcc 11.2.0 -O3 -march=native, Intel i9-9940X, one thread, human genome with 2.5 billion 31-mers), canonical SSHash answered streaming membership in 253/183 ns per k-mer (high/low hit rate), against 402/435 ns for Pufferfish dense and 440/1,088 ns for BLight. It used 9.39 bits/k-mer (vs 45.04 and 20.17) and built in 16.2 min (vs 70.7 and 25.0), but its random lookups (990/854 ns) were slower than Pufferfish dense (720/519 ns); no standard-library baseline was involved, and only the SSHash side of that harness is public.
status_note: Actively maintained (v6.0.0 shipped 2026-08-29 with a breaking index-format change; last commit 2026-09-03), MIT-licensed, on Bioconda with a Rust port, and consumed as a CMake static-library target with submodules rather than a header-only drop.
